title: Binary search trees
summary: Search, insert, and delete in O(h); without balance, h can be n.

parts.rule: In a binary search tree every left descendant is less than the node and every right descendant is greater. Search, insert, and delete run in time O(h) where h is the height. Balanced trees keep h near log n; inserting keys in sorted order builds a stick of height n. Always say height, not "log n for free."
parts.why: Candidates recite "BST is logarithmic" as if balance were automatic. Interviewers ask what happens when keys arrive sorted, or how delete finds an inorder successor. Separating the BST order property from a balanced variant is the difference between a correct cost story and a hopeful one.
parts.example: Insert 5, then 3, then 7, then 4 into an empty tree. Five becomes the root. Three goes left of five. Seven goes right of five. Four goes right of three. Search for four: compare with five (go left), compare with three (go right), find four in three steps while height is about two. Now insert one, then two, then three into a fresh empty tree in ascending order: each new key goes right, so three nodes form a chain of height three — linear in n. Delete three from the first tree when three has one child four: replace three with four under five. If a node has two children, copy the inorder successor (minimum of the right subtree) into the node, then delete that successor, which has at most one child.
parts.use: Use a BST when you need ordered keys plus dynamic insert and delete, and you can keep or assume balance. Use inorder traversal to emit sorted keys without an extra sort pass. Use it when range queries over keys matter more than raw hash speed.
parts.refuse: Refuse promising O(log n) without a balance story when inputs can be sorted. Refuse a raw BST when a hash map suffices and order is never used. Refuse deleting a two-child node by only nulling pointers without successor handling. Refuse confusing heap shape with BST key order.

body:
Rule. In a binary search tree every left descendant is less than the node and every right descendant is greater. Search, insert, and delete run in time O(h) where h is the height. Balanced trees keep h near log n; inserting keys in sorted order builds a stick of height n. Always say height, not "log n for free."

Why it matters. Candidates recite "BST is logarithmic" as if balance were automatic. Interviewers ask what happens when keys arrive sorted, or how delete finds an inorder successor. Separating the BST order property from a balanced variant is the difference between a correct cost story and a hopeful one.

Worked example. Insert 5, then 3, then 7, then 4 into an empty tree. Five becomes the root. Three goes left of five. Seven goes right of five. Four goes right of three. Search for four: compare with five (go left), compare with three (go right), find four in three steps while height is about two. Now insert one, then two, then three into a fresh empty tree in ascending order: each new key goes right, so three nodes form a chain of height three — linear in n. Delete three from the first tree when three has one child four: replace three with four under five. If a node has two children, copy the inorder successor (minimum of the right subtree) into the node, then delete that successor, which has at most one child.

When to use. Use a BST when you need ordered keys plus dynamic insert and delete, and you can keep or assume balance. Use inorder traversal to emit sorted keys without an extra sort pass. Use it when range queries over keys matter more than raw hash speed.

When to refuse. Refuse promising O(log n) without a balance story when inputs can be sorted. Refuse a raw BST when a hash map suffices and order is never used. Refuse deleting a two-child node by only nulling pointers without successor handling. Refuse confusing heap shape with BST key order.
